sentences.text: The wind blew all through the third day.
Farmor watched the light fade in the afternoon.
She was quiet.
She did not ask Nell what she had planned to offer.
Perhaps she did not want to interfere.
Perhaps she was afraid Nell had made the wrong choice, the way she had.
At eleven o'clock at night, Nell put on her boots and her coat and her hat.
"Farmor," she said.
"I need to do this on my own."
Farmor did not argue.
She only nodded, once, and put the small wooden offering box in Nell's hands.
"Then take this," she said.
"Whatever you give — put it inside.
That's the way it's done."
Nell opened the front door.
The cold came in like a slap.
The wind was very loud.
The snow in the yard was so bright with moonlight that it hurt to look at.
She stepped out onto the doorstep.
She closed the door softly behind her.
The tracks from the last two nights were still there, filling in with fresh snow.
New tracks led up to the doorstep from the trees.
Nell looked up.
The fox was there.
It was smaller than she had expected.
A pure white arctic fox, with the softest-looking fur she had ever seen.
Its eyes were the color of amber — a warm, dark gold.
It sat very still in the snow, three feet from her, and it looked at her.
Nell's heart was beating very hard.
She did not know if the fox understood people.
She did not know if it understood English.
She did not know if it understood anything.
She only knew what she was going to try.
She put the small wooden offering box down on the doorstep.
Then she took a deep, shaky breath, and she began to sing.
The song was a lullaby.
It was the one her mother had sung to her when she was very small, before Nell could remember words.
It was a Swedish lullaby, one her mother had learned from Farmor.
Nell did not remember all the words.
She sang the ones she knew and hummed the ones she didn't.
"Vem kan segla förutan vind," she sang, quietly.
"Vem kan ro utan åror.
Vem kan skiljas från vännen sin, utan att fälla tårar."
Her voice shook.
She kept going.
The fox listened.
It did not move.
Its amber eyes stayed on Nell's face.
The wind, which had been so loud, seemed to grow softer, as if the trees themselves were listening.
Nell sang all four verses that she could remember.
When she finished, she stood very still.
The song hung in the cold air.
The fox got to its feet.
It walked to the offering box.
It looked at it.
Then it looked back at Nell.
It bowed its head, once — slowly, deliberately, like someone accepting a gift with great respect.
And then it turned and disappeared into the trees.
Nell stood on the doorstep for a long time after the fox was gone.
The wind was still blowing.
The moon was still bright.
But something had changed.
She could feel it.
She picked up the offering box.
It was still empty — she had not put anything in it.
She had thought that was what she was going to do.
But when the moment came, she had not.
The song had been the gift.
The box had been the way to say: this counts as an offering.
Please receive it.
The fox had received it.
Inside, Farmor was waiting by the fire.
She looked up when Nell came in, and she looked at the empty box in Nell's hands, and her eyes filled with tears.
"You sang."
"I sang the lullaby that Mama used to sing me."
Farmor put her hand over her mouth.
"That was my mother's song," she said.
"She sang it to your mother.
Your mother sang it to you.
I never — I never thought to sing it to the fox."
Nell sat down beside her.
Farmor put an arm around her shoulders.
The next morning, Farmor got a fresh piece of paper.
In her careful, spidery handwriting, she wrote down the four verses of the lullaby that Nell had sung.
She folded the paper and put it inside the small wooden offering box.
She closed the lid.
"For the next one," she said.
"In case there is a long time before the wind comes again.
In case whoever comes next does not remember the words."
She put the box back in the drawer.
Outside, the wind had finally stopped.
The trees stood still.
Somewhere far off in the forest, a small white fox was making its way home, carrying something very quietly, that only it could hear.
